utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They sent a courier who brought with him the call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know what would happen to anybody who refused to respond to what you've termed a "call-up paper"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They would be beaten up and sent to the frontline nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there another time in 1995 where you were once again sent to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: On that occasion, the Serb police came early in the morning and picked up me, Dursum Pajic, Zijad Bukvic, Dervis Sehic, Safet Sehic, Mehmed Sehic, Osman Muratovic, and took us directly to a place called Drenovo Kisela [phoen] not far from the Grabez barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on this occasion, how long did you remain working at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Until the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention once again to your work at the frontline in 1993. Can you tell us what types of tasks were you given to complete during your time at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We had to dig trenches, to fortify those trenches, to carry food for the Serb troops, water, and other heavy labour that needed to be done, we had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And once again, in -- from May to September of 1995, did you have similar tasks or did you have any different tasks to perform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, in the breaks, when we didn't go to the battlefield, we would do work in my village. For instance, we had to cut wood for the families of killed Serb combatants and various other activities, like cutting the hay, the grass, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in September of 1995, can I ask you to explain to the Chamber in terms of context, what was going on in the Bihac area and in the Sanski Most area at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: On the 13th of September, the forces of the 5th Corps of the BH army penetrated and broke through Serb lines, so that the Serb army started withdrawing towards Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present working on the frontline when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you and the other people there -- or the other Bosniaks there on work obligation do when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We had to go together with the Serb army towards Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Sanski Most, were you given any instructions by the Serbs in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Before we reached the town itself, the soldiers who were from Kljuc left us at the very entrance to Sanski Most. Then we were taken over by soldiers from Drvar, whose intention it was to take us somewhere to the battlefront at Manjaca. However, they also left us behind there, saying that the order was that they couldn't take us with them. Just then we learnt that the Kljuc troops or army that we belonged to under work obligation was stationed in a place called Poljak, not far from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this period of time, from May 1995 up until the time you're describing for us now, were you free to leave your work obligation and go where you pleased?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Poljak, near the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you do when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we arrived there, we first washed in a stream. Then we found a stable to stay in. Just then a soldier arrived, or shortly after that, with a nice clean uniform on him, a camouflage uniform; whereas, the other Serb soldiers that we belonged to under work obligation were not so nicely dressed. And he asked the soldiers from Kljuc to give him a vehicle and men to load ammunition from the Veleprom warehouse and to drive it in front of the Sanus Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few more questions about that soldier. You've described him as wearing a camouflage uniform. Did you see whether or not he had any insignia or identifying markings on his camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Just then I didn't, but the soldiers from Kljuc asked him, "And who is that ammunition and weapons for that we are going to take?" And he answered that it was for Commander Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've described yourself as being present when he addressed you and some others. Was there anything distinctive about his dialect, his manner of speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed immediately that this soldier was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to tell that he was from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Because he used the Ekavian dialect in his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that a dialect that is unique to people from a particular part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this soldier armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was he armed with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: He had an automatic rifle on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that he was requesting a vehicle to transport munitions from the Veleprom factory. Can you please describe for the Chamber, what is the Veleprom factory and where it's located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: It is a warehouse, Veleprom, situated in Poljak, not far from Sanski Most, about a kilometre from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified he wanted to transport these munitions to the Hotel Sanus. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: The hotel is in the centre of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after he made this request for a vehicle to move these munitions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: A Serb soldier - his surname was Vojvodic - told us that we should go and load the weapons from Veleprom, drive it to the Sanus Hotel, after which we would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This Vojvodic, when you say a Serb soldier, do you mean a soldier from Serbia or a local Bosnian Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: From the ranks of Bosnian Serbs. I knew him well. He's from Kljuc. But I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go -- did you do as he instructed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the way to Veleprom, did you hear any conversation between this soldier and the other local soldiers or Bosnian Serb soldiers regarding the purpose of Arkan's men coming to the Sanski Most area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that conversation. Arkan's soldiers said that they had come to Sanski Most with the task of regaining control of Kljuc, which had been taken by the 5th Corps, that is, the soldiers of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe who was present on the truck, not necessarily the names but just give us some idea of who was on the truck as it went to Veleprom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: There was this soldier Vojvodic and Arkan's soldier, who had come to fetch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at Veleprom warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We found there five or six of Arkan's soldiers, who ordered us to load the ammunition, some mortar barrels as well that were there, and even some stretchers for the wounded. They kept telling us to hurry up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how much time did you spend at the Veleprom warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: About half an hour, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened after the truck was loaded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Then we headed towards the Sanus Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to travel from Veleprom to the Sanus Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22487 to 22493. Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the Sanus Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the hotel itself, at the parking lot I noticed some tanks, APCs, mortars, and in front there were about ten or so of Arkan's soldiers there all the time. Across the way from the hotel itself, in front of a building, I saw some civilians that were tied up. They were tied to some pillars. Then they told us to wait, because we couldn't unload the truck until the commander arrived and the commander was somewhere in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see any busses in the parking lot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there anything on the busses to indicate where they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. It said "Vukovar" on them. I am not quite sure whether it was Autoprevoz Vukovar, but I am sure that the word "Vukovar" was written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the men you've described as being members of Arkan's unit, how were you able to identify them as such?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Because the soldier from Kljuc spoke to one of Arkan's soldiers. They spoke at length, to the effect that they have come there to regain control of Kljuc, that the commander was in the field. They used the Ekavian dialect in their speech and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to or did you form an impression regarding the relationship between Arkan's men and the local Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Afterwards I came to the conclusion that they were not on the best of terms, as the local soldiers were fleeing, whereas Arkan's soldiers rounded them up and brought them to the Sanus Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned two men being tied to a pole in this area. Did there come a time when you found out what happened, why these men were tied to a pole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: The Arkan's soldier explained to soldier Vojvodic that they were men that Arkan had found drunk in Sanski Most, and that is why he had tied them to this pole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you learn their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a person by the name of Mr. Rasula, the president of Sanski Most, addressed you and other -- the other people you were with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman came to the truck where we were sitting, and he asked whether any one of us had been drinking alcohol during the day. If somebody had been drinking alcohol, then they should watch out for Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how is it that you recognised Mr. Rasula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Rasula often on television, so I immediately recognised him when he walked up to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 468, tab 2. It is two photographs that will be displayed on a television screen before you. If you have any difficulty seeing them, let us know and we'll provide the original photographs. Do you recognise the locations depicted in both of these photographs? And I'd ask you to start by telling us about the photograph on the top, ending in number 110.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what do you recognise that to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: On the first photograph, we see the very entrance into the Hotel Sanus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to describe what is depicted in the second photograph, ending in ERN number 11, 1-1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: In the second photograph, the door can be seen, the one that leads into the room where Mr. Arkan had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the Sanus Hotel, did you begin to unload the weapons and munitions that were on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, not immediately. We had to wait for Arkan to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did you wait before -- did there come a time when Arkan did come? And if so, how long did you wait?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: As soon as it was dusk, a soldier came and said that the truck could park in front of Sanus, and that's when we started unloading the ammunition and the other goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you bring the ammunition and other goods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We brought it into the Sanus Hotel. This is a door that is different from the one that I showed in the picture, where Arkan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened after you unloaded the weapons and other goods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we were just about to finish unloading this, a soldier told us finally that we would go into the hotel and that we would be examined by Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go into the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where precisely in the hotel did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Right behind the entrance door there was a pool table. We were ordered to line up by that pool table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw in that area of the hotel at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we got in, I saw an old man who was cutting the hair of Serb soldiers. This man was a Bosniak. The soldiers were stopping -- were standing in a line, and he was shaving their heads. I noticed that they were then taken into the busses that were out in front. I think that they were returned to the frontline yet again then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the purpose of shaving their heads, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I assume that quite simply these are soldiers who were being marked for being deserters, for running away, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was Arkan present in that part of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan got out through the first door that I showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did he say at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: He asked who these people were. A soldier said that these were the men who had unloaded the ammunition. He then walked up to soldier Vojvodic. He asked him who he was. He answered, he gave his name and surname. He asked him three times, and then he said that he could go and that we should stay. Then he asked us individually what our names were. After that he showed us a hall and told us to stand there, to wait, and that there would be work for us and that we would be engaged in doing this work. That's exactly what we did. We went to that hall and stood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In this part of the hotel, how many men were there that were not part of the local Serb army and were not members of the group that you were with? Can you tell us approximately how many men were there and describe what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Aside from yourself, the men in your group, and any local Serb soldiers, can you describe who else was present in the lobby of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Arkan's soldiers were there. They were going up and down the stairs. So I don't know what the exact number was. They kept going up and down. Then this man who was shaving people's heads, and in the meantime some other men were brought in front of the hotel. I didn't really see. I just heard some noise, some clamoring. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say Arkan at this point in time, was he wearing anything on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you remember seeing any insignia on that beret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On the beret, there were four Cyrillic S's, and then the letters saying "Serbian Volunteer Guard" were in a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other men with Arkan, do you recall what, if anything, they were wearing on their heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Some wore black berets; others had black woollen camps. While, the ones who were closer to Arkan, I think, all had red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you saw somebody who you believed was a colonel or a lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe that person as best you can for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: The man was rather short. His hair was cut short. He was sturdily built. He walked into the toilet and the door leading to the toilet was opposite where we were standing. As he was walking back from the toilet, he looked straight at me. He then asked me whether I was a Turk. But his tone of voice was such that I simply had to answer yes. He asked me three times. Every time he was speaking louder and louder, and every time I answered him. Then he told me to sit down. I sat down on the tiles, on the floor. He told me that I was supposed to sit like Turks sat when they wanted to dine, that I should cross my legs, and that's exactly what I did. Then he said that I should lower my head as far as I could, close to the floor, and then he told everybody else to do so too. Then he placed a soldier in front of us and said that if any one of us moved, that the soldier should shoot us with a bullet in our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did you remain there in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, until 2.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many other Bosniaks or Muslims were in the room with you in -- sitting down in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Seven more Bosniaks were brought in, and then there were the five of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when two Muslims or two Bosniaks were brought into the room and accused of celebrating in advance of the Bosnian army's success in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Then Arkan ordered these soldiers who had brought them in to tie them up outside to some trees that were in front of the Sanus Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the people that were present in the hotel, are you able to say whether or not Arkan spoke with each of the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Every man who was brought in first had to stand in front of Arkan and speak to him, so I came to the conclusion that nothing should happen there without him knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a local Serb major had a discussion with Arkan regarding granting vacation leave to another soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. When a soldier was brought in by Arkan's men, said that he had received permission from the major to leave the frontline. After that, Arkan immediately issued orders to have this major brought to the Sanus Hotel, which is exactly what his men did. When the major arrived, I heard Arkan saying to him, "How can you let men go when the situation is the most difficult for the Serb people? I brought my own son, and he's up there at the frontline."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this point in time, Arkan had no legal authority over VRS soldiers. Did you form an impression regarding -- or strike that. Did this major or any of his men protest or resist Arkan when he called the major before him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified earlier about a barber shaving the heads of Serb deserters. Approximately how many men altogether had their head shaves while you were present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I could not give you an exact number, because at one point in time -- I mean, I was there, sitting with my head down for five or six hours, so I couldn't really see. But they were being brought in all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you and other men in the group were ordered to unload a truck outside the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, we heard a truck coming up to the entrance. Then they told us to get up and to unload something outside. I and many others could not readily get to their feet because quite simply our legs were numb because we had sat that way for so long. When we somehow managed to get up and reach the truck, we saw some books there, some kind of archives. We heard in passing that these were the archives of the Party of Democratic Action that were found in Sanski Most. We were told that we should unload this quickly and pile it up in front of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What time of the day was this, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: It was around 2.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what day was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't remember the day. I remember the date though. It was the morning of the 20th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after you unloaded these SDA files?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We were told to go back to the place where we were supposed to be. I was the first one to go to that hall. All of a sudden we heard the following: "Go back. They have to go back." At that moment, when we turned around to go back, I was the last man in that line. When I got outside, I saw them tying men in pairs, the men from my group, and they brought them onto a truck. They were actually handcuffing everyone, so they handcuffed me as well. I was handcuffed to a man I didn't know. We boarded the truck. At that moment, they were looking for some Zeljo. "Where is Zeljo?" And he was supposed to go with us. When this Zeljo arrived, I saw that he couldn't have been older than 15 or 16. He was very young. He wore a uniform which was the same like the uniform worn by all of the other men, Arkan's men. Then they put the tarpaulin down, three of these soldiers sat with us underneath the tarpaulin. And then they ignited the truck and we set out in a direction that we were not aware of. We drove on for about half an hour that way, and then the truck stopped. From the truck cab we heard them getting out. Then they lifted the tarpaulin. And then these three soldiers jumped off the truck, and soon they said, "Come on. Get off, you two." These two got off. And soon two gunshots were heard. According to the sound, I could tell that they were shooting indoors. Soon after that, these same persons returned to the truck. I asked one of them very softly what happened to them. But he just put his finger on his lips; I noticed that. And he kept quiet. And then they said, "Next." Again, two gunshots were heard, but they did not return to the truck. So my turn came as well. I got off the truck, together with the man to whom I had been handcuffed. Then they took us by a house that did not have a roof. Behind it we saw a smaller house with a garage. They took us into the garage. One of them started taking off our handcuffs, and the other one had a torchlight on. At that moment I said, "People, can you not kill us somehow?" And then Arkan's soldier said, "Yes. You're lucky. You're lucky to be in Arkan's hands. Give us 5.000 Deutschmark each, get into the truck, and we'll drive you to your homes." At that moment I said that I was from Kljuc. While the other man who was handcuffed said that he had 200 Deutschmark. He swore at these 200 Deutschmark and said that we should get into this little room that was within this garage. Then I looked in the direction where the man -- the soldier had his torchlight on. I saw bodies lying. I saw pools of blood. So I turned around together with this man and walked inside. As soon as I got in, a bullet hit me in my left shoulder and -- shoulder blade and I immediately fell to the ground. I kept quiet. Then they brought two more men, and I heard just one gunshot. Then one of Arkan's soldiers started swearing at this man who had fallen before a bullet was fired into him. Then I heard the soldier start his weapon, opening a burst of gunfire at this man. One bullet went through my left leg. Then they brought those two men who had left the truck first and were subsequently returned. I heard them order them to kneel. One of them was begging, "Don't, please." And the other one started swearing at him and said, "Kneel, Bre." Then I heard a knife being taken out of the scabbard and then this soldier said, "Zeljo, you can do the honours. You can do the best part of the job." This young soldier of Arkan's slit the throats of these two men. Then we could hear other people gurgling in that pile of human bodies. And then one of Arkan's soldiers said, "Well, some of them are still alive. We heard a voice." And then another voice said, "Well, just shoot them in the head." So the light fell on my face too. I heard a gunshot then, and I was hit in the chin, on the right side in the chin area. Then they boarded the truck. And when I heard them leave, when I heard the truck leaving, I asked whether anybody was still alive. I put this question several times; however, nobody answered. Since my left arm was numb, I put my left hand on my belt, the belt on my trousers, and I somehow managed to get up. I got out of that room and set out towards the road. I thought I could not take this for very long. I thought I'd die very soon, so I wanted to be somewhere by the road so that someone could find me. From time to time, I couldn't see anything, and then I could see again. And at one point I felt very thirsty. So I started walking along the road, trying to find some water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let counsel ask some questions now to clarify any matters and also possibly to shorten things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, how many men were led off the truck and shot in that room that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Twelve men were taken. Eleven were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And of those 12 men, how many of them whose names did you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They were Mehmed Sehic, Safet Sehic, Dervis Sehic, and Osman Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were any of these men who were killed, were any of them close friends of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I would say Mehmed Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at some photographs. The first one is Prosecution Exhibit 468, tab 3. It's the house that has a photograph -- it's a photograph of a house. I'd ask you to look at it on the television screen before you and ask you: Do you recognise that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what you recognise it to be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: In front of this first building the truck that brought us was parked. And behind this bigger building is the smaller building where the massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to tab 4 of 468. And I'd ask you: You recognise the building in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the garage through which you would enter a small room where they executed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, if you would take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 468, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: That's precisely the room I mentioned where the massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned being shot. How many times altogether or how many gunshot wounds altogether did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Three bullets hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you summarise again where on your body you sustained those gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: One bullet hit me in the left shoulder by my collarbone, next to my collarbone. The second one hit me in my chin. And the third hit my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at four photographs which make up -- I'm sorry, five photographs which make up Prosecution Exhibit 468, tab 6. Are these photographs of the injuries that you've described here in your testimony? I'm sorry, your answer wasn't --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you received extensive medical treatment for these injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on, Mr. Groome, I think we should clarify whereabouts the house and garage are, so that we have that located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, at the time of the massacre, did you know where it was that you had been brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: At that point in time, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did learn where it was that this massacre took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I learnt that later on from one of the soldiers at Kljuc to whom I told what had happened to me, and he said that that place was called Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know where that location is with respect to the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly how many kilometres away it is, but it's not far from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 468, and my question to you is: Are these the medical records of the treatment you received for the injuries you sustained that night?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you: Did you suffer any permanent consequences from the injuries you sustained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. I'm 60 per cent an invalid, and I will be for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would now ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 468, tab 8. Do you recognise what this document is? What I recognise here are the people who were shot, not all of them, but some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the names that you told us the people you knew, do their names appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 3, Osman Muratovic; number 4, Safet Sehic; number 5, Mehmed Sehic; and then number 9, Dervis Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Last week were you asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Last week were you asked to look at a videotape of a number of corpses, the video being taken by some investigators from the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you recognise some of the names on the name tags on the bodies as well as some of the clothing that was worn in that video by the victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised the names, and I recognised the clothing worn by Mehmed Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for the record what that clothing looked like in the video.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I remembered the jumper Mehmed Sehic was wearing very well, but I couldn't recognise the rest because the bodies were already disintegrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were any of the bodies -- or did any of the people who were shot that day have on military uniforms or were they armed in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, nobody was wearing a military uniform nor were they armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that at least a portion of this video be played for the witness to establish that it was the video he looked at earlier or last week. It's a five and a half minute video. I'm not sure that the Chamber would want the entire video played. But I'll be guided by the Chamber on how much of the video is played for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you select the passages which you think most appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I will play the first 30 seconds so he can establish that it was the video that he looked at in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at the video screen in front of you, and we will now play the video. And I will ask you to confirm whether or not it's the video you viewed last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise this video, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you need to look at more of it to -- to tell us with certainty whether it's the video that you saw in which you recognised the clothing and the names of the other people that were killed on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, that's the footage. And those are the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We can stop the video now. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1047, on page 2, paragraph 5 of your statement you say that the Serbs took Kljuc in April 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who did the Serbs seize Kljuc from, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they proclaimed the police force the Serb police, and the Bosniaks and Croats from the police force they expelled. Then in the municipality all the Bosniaks and Croats were sacked and their jobs -- in their jobs were put people of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any personal knowledge about the fact that all Croats and Muslims were sacked, dismissed from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I know for sure that nobody worked after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Serbs lived in Kljuc before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the fighting around Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was a Muslim Crisis Staff set up in Kljuc, as it was in other places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that because I wasn't able to go to Kljuc. You needed a special permit if you wanted to go into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about before April 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to have a special permit to go into town before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please - and I'm talking about the time before April 1992, when, as you say, the Serbs took control of Kljuc - so before that time in Kljuc was there an organisation that was called the Patriotic League that was functioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, were you in the town of Kljuc at all before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you take part in any activities on the part of the Muslim forces in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of Muslim forces in Kljuc before April 1992, that they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see anybody there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can see from your statement that you stayed in your own village after April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a purely Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the Muslims leave your village at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you all stayed on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. If you mean during the war, whether anybody left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, a lot of people did leave my village. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you remained? How come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, I remained because when I wanted to get my travelling papers, they stopped this process and said that nobody was allowed to leave any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't allow the population to leave the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They kept back some of the inhabitants so that those inhabitants could do the dirtiest jobs. And even some Serbs confirmed this because this was to show the world that they were not actually expelling the Muslim, Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they said that you should stay so that they could demonstrate to the world that they weren't expelling the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 2, paragraphs 5 and 6 you say that you had a work assignment which included various jobs either up at the frontline or in Kljuc itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you had to dig trenches and a moment ago said you had to fetch and carry for the army food and water and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you happen to know that a work obligation or task was something that was assigned to the Serbs too who weren't part of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, they did have a labour obligation, but in companies in town, where they had worked prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that they were given a choice, either to join up, to join the army, or to accept this work obligation or labour obligation which was compulsory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We weren't offered to take up arms and join the army. That wasn't the choice we had. All they did was to make us do our labour obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about the Serbs. Did you know that the Serbs had a choice that they could either join up or have a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, please: As you say you drug trenches, fetch and carried for the army food and water and so on, did you eat and were you supplied with food like the army was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you live? In your village throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you would go home regularly, after you had performed your labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Not regularly, no. We would do our work for a month or two and then go home. And soon as we would arrive home, the local Serbs would engage us to do some tasks for them and we didn't dare say no, refuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were going back to your village after your labour obligation and then came back, were you escorted under armed forces or were you free to move around, to go back to your village freely and then back again to your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we would come back from Kljuc itself, having accomplished our obligation, we would go alone. But we were escorted to Kljuc by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you would come in when some jobs had to be done and then they would come and fetch you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Would you repeat that? I'm not sure I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying you would go into Kljuc when somebody came to call you to go to Kljuc, and then you'd go to Kljuc with them. But on the return journey for your free time you would go alone. That's how I understood it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I made a note of this here from what you were saying. In the village, when you were in your village, you would chop wood, you would mow the fields and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, and repair the local roads and paths, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you have an obligation to wear any kind of uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during that period of time, while you were in your own village, did you live normally, watch television, live like anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: During the daytime, you could live like anybody else. But at night we had to sleep in the meadows and fields, in the gardens and yards, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But if you went back to your village, I assume you slept in the village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you slept at home, in your own house, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I've just said we didn't dare sleep in our own homes, or very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned the mayor of Sanski Most, Rasula, and said that you had seen him on television many times. So where were you watching television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We were able to watch television from time to time because there wasn't electricity on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you watched television in your own home, not in fields, meadows, woods, or wherever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, yes, and we watched it in the house of a good colleague of ours. I don't want to mention his name. We're still very good friends, and he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So throughout that time, you were wearing civilian clothes. You never had any army uniforms or insignia or anything of that kind, as far as I understood it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior when you went about your obligations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: He was Drago Ivanovic. That was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I think he was the head of the civil defence and Territorial Defence. I think civil defence, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these various work obligations and jobs, like repairing roads and various other things, did that come under the Territorial Defence tasks, civil defence tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: But not escorted by armed personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you a member of a unit within the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When we went to the frontline, for a time we were sent to the Drvar army, and the rest of the time with the Kljuc army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you performed your work obligations either within the unit of Republika Srpska from Drvar or from Kljuc; is that right? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I was able to gather, mostly under the Kljuc unit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: When you were performing these work obligations, was there any fighting going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you present when there was fighting or combat going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you see happen? Who was fighting whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: The fighting was between the army to which we belonged, within the frameworks of our work obligation, and the army -- the soldiers of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the frontline between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I understand it, you didn't have the status of a prisoner of war at all. You said yourself you were free to move around and you engaged in this work organisation as a citizen of the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by "free to move around," when we were always under guard, armed persons escorting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said a moment ago when you were done your work obligation, were free to leave and to go to your village that nobody escorted you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. But we went home at great risk. We were always very much afraid that we wouldn't meet somebody on the road home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that if you were allowed to go home, that you didn't flee. You had permission to return home. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you get to a convenient time, we're going to break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. It's time for the break. Well, that's fine, Mr. May. We can break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Witness B-1047, we're going to break now for 20 minutes. Could you remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have three-quarters of an hour left if you want for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1047, since you were staying in your own house at that time, where was your family at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: In the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Occasionally they had problems, until a Serb spared us and helped us and relieved us of many of those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in 1995 you were assigned to a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska from Kljuc that was accommodated in Poljak, a village close to Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, that is where they were quartered, after they had withdrawn from the Bihac battlefront.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then following orders, you went to Poljak to find your unit commanders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Not following orders. We set off on our own, because we had no other choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you set off on your own and no one was escorting you, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Through the town itself, no one. But up to the town, there were six soldiers accompanying us always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But over there you were free, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: In the town itself, we were free to pass through to reach Poljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far is Poljak from the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I think about 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as you were passing through the town itself, going to Poljak, there was no armed escort that could prevent you from escaping if you had decided to do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, were you forced to go there? Why didn't you escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Because we didn't know which direction to take in fleeing, because there were troops everywhere around us and we didn't know who was where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how do you explain the fact that together with other members of your group you were moving freely in territory under control of the Serb force and you reported to the unit commander to whom you had been assigned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: We had been left to our own resources, and we simply had to go through the town on our own. That was the only choice we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, looking at a videotape, you recognised bodies, though I didn't have the impression that one could recognise anything on that tape. But I would now like you to look at a tape and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it won't take more than a minute. It was taken in those days in the surroundings of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I will put a question to you in advance. That is, my question is: Do you recognise anyone on the tape? Do you know who they were? As you can see them very clearly, unlike what we saw on the previous tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Have you surrendered? Do you know me? No, I don't. Where are you from? What do you mean you don't know? Who is he? The army. And where are they from? From different countries. And why are they coming? They're coming to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We do not have a transcript and it is very hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] You don't have to live at all, I will kill you, the killer promised. That is how on the 16th of October -- these were Serbs. Who's going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can stop now. That is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are Serb victims. Did you recognise this warrant officer who was captured and later on slaughtered there? And did you recognise any of the men around him from the 5th Corps corps? This was filmed by a cameraman of the 5th Corps of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I did not recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 4, paragraph 3 you say - and on page 5, first paragraph - you describe the events while you were at the Sanus Hotel in Sanski Most and you describe the conversation between Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and a certain JNA officer -- no, I'm sorry, an officer of the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a moment ago you said that Raznjatovic criticised this officer for allowing his soldiers to go home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was all this happening at the time when the VRS was withdrawing after the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the NATO bombing because it didn't happen in the parts where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you quoted - and I noted down here - that Arkan said, "How dare you allow men to go on leave when the situation is so difficult? I've brought my son here, and he's on the frontline."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in that chaos he was even trying to keep hold of the line. He even brought his son who on the frontline could also have been killed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness can't answer that. It's merely what Arkan said. Whether it's true or not is not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this young soldier that you describe, he was sent back to the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when this was happening, you were still a captive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you then manage to hear the conversation between Arkan and this soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Because the conversation was taking place a couple of metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were all present and you heard that conversation, your whole group. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you say that they also discussed some other things, tell us, what other things did they discuss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I personally don't know what else they talked about, but this I remembered very well, and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the conversation wasn't in an office but in the corridor, where you were all present.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was happening in Arkan's office that you mentioned that was right next to the entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that anyone else went inside except for Arkan, who would go inside occasionally into that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 3 of your statement, you say that members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, that is, Arkan's Guards, after completing their work assignments had -- tied you up two by two and loaded you onto a truck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after transferring you to a particular place, two men from the truck were taken in an unknown direction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you heard two shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, those two returned safe and sound and climbed onto the truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever explain this situation to yourself? Because you say later on that there were executions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I came to the conclusion that this was done for us to believe that that is how we, too, would fair, that we would return safe and sound to the truck so as not to provoke panic which would prompt us to try to flee or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the trailer, were any members of Arkan's unit with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you asked those two what had happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, quietly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, with another person, you were taken to a spot where you say executions took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I was the fourth in order. I was the fourth to get off the truck. There were three pairs in front of us and then the two of us got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is where you saw those men killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, when they showed us to go inside, I looked around, and I saw those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Since you had your back turned to the soldiers that were shooting at you, how many soldiers were shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They shot individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many were there in all in the truck with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: There were three soldiers with us under a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who -- which unit did those soldiers belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: They were Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All three of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Because they spoke the Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that when they -- when you were climbing up onto the truck they said that a young man was due to come and you said he was 15 or 16 and they called him Zeljo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Zeljo, as you know, is not a name used in Serbia but exclusively in Bosnia. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Serbia it would be either Zeljko or something like that. But Zeljo is more typical of Bosnia. As you are making this distinction in the speech people used, so you could tell they were from Serbia. But Zeljo couldn't be from Serbia, could he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I really don't know that. But I claim with full responsibility that they used the word "Zeljo."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe you, but I'm just asking whether you know that Zeljo could not have been from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance from which they opened fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Well, a maximum of one and a half metres to two. As soon as you enter the room -- as soon as you entered the room, they would open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, as something is not quite clear to me: You were given here a list, and on it there are 11 names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we were looking at the tape shown to you by Mr. Groome only a part of it was shown, but as the camera covered the scene they reached the number 19. How can you identify that tape where there were at least 19, because we saw the numbers - there could have been more - with the people that you identified and who are on this list of 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't know at all what those numbers mean, but I did see below the numbers the names of the people who were executed at the time and whom I knew, and I recognised the one among them by his pullover, and he is Mehmed Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The one you recognised was from your group, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As there were three soldiers there, someone called Zeljo and another two that you claim were Arkan's men, do you believe that they did this of their own free will or following somebody's orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Absolutely not. In my view, nothing could occur without Arkan's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even if he wasn't present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes. They had to wait for him before doing anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you now please look at -- it is tab 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume you won't show the picture, Mr. May, on the screen, because the witness can be seen on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The picture is very clear, so please look at it. Will you please find it. It is in tab 6. It's the first photograph following the medical reports. It's marked 00474104. You have explained -- I hope you can see the picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see the wound near the collarbone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And nowhere can you see the wound on the chin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it on this first photograph, if you look a little more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I do look more closely, then even if this hardly visible dot on the chin could be that wound, wouldn't -- could it differ from the one on the clavicle? Because this one is very visible. It clearly -- it can clearly be seen that it was made very briefly prior to the taking of the photograph. So wouldn't the other one -- shouldn't the other one look similar to that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when the photographs were taken; however, this wound near the collarbone that you see, I had problems with it for a whole year, because it wouldn't heal. And that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I may assist. The date that the photograph was taken has actually been printed on the photograph itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, July -- it seems to be July 1996. But the witness isn't a doctor. He can't help us to medical matters. He can only say what he himself suffered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But where is the exit wound, if this is the wound on the chin that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: At the time, I had the luck in this tragedy for the bullet just to scathe me. There was a lot of bleeding, but you can't see it too well on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I won't bother you with any more questions about that, because clearly there's a difference between the appearance of the wound on the chin and the other one on the collarbone. But tell me, please: As we see on these -- we don't see on these photographs, but you also were hit in the hip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No, in my leg, the upper leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you started running, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you manage to escape? When they had finished everything and the truck left or before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: When I heard that the truck was moving away from the spot, I got up and moved away from that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, you heard one soldier order another to shoot everyone in the head, and he's the one who hit you in the chin; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had the good luck that he missed you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I can't say that he missed me, but -- he did hit me, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Judging by what it says here, that when they established that all of you had been killed, they left the spot and you then heard somebody's moans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I see here that you say that the man who was moaning, as you yourself say, had a big hole on his forehead. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He wasn't moaning. He was just gurgling. That's all you could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you explain that a man who has a big hole and a direct hit in the forehead is not dead on the spot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not for the witness to guess that. As I say, he's not a doctor. All he can say is what he saw and heard himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from your statement, after you were wounded you walked all day, you spent the night under a plum tree in an orchard, and then you arrived in Poljak on the 21st of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During those two days, did you ever pass out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you use anything to bandage your wound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spent a night underneath a plum tree in an orchard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to get some sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: I don't think I got any sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Mr. Groome examined you along the lines of your statement up to a certain point, up to this point. And now I'm going to read out to you what you said on page 7 of your statement in this second paragraph, if we do not count the one that started on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his statement. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what it says. This is the second paragraph, if we do not count the paragraph that started on the previous page. So this is page 7 of your statement. This is what it says: "I arrived in Poljak around noon the following day, on the 21st of September, 1995. As I expected, the Serb army was there." So you were hurrying to Poljak to come to a unit where the Army of Republika Srpska was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you proceed, you say, "Near one of the houses I saw a group of soldiers and approached them. As they observed me, there was great consternation among them. I must have looked appalling, all covered in blood, since there was nothing I could have done for my wounds."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "I passed them and climbed on the barn where there was still my bag with my clothes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you move on to say: "Djoko Mladjenovic showed up soon. He was a Serb but a good colleague of mine, and I was sure he would not give me away, so I told him all what happened."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "I described the village and its location and he said that it was Trnova. He gave me some food and then went to see the commanding officer, a certain Malic" -- I do not know his name or rank -- "in order to try to get me to a hospital."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you say that he would not give you away, could you please explain that to me. You came there and everybody saw you come. Everybody saw you covered with blood, and you went to get your bag. It was a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. So nobody could assume that you came secretly. Everybody saw you, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This friend of yours went to the commander -- to his commanding officer and asked for you to be taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say further on: "Malic said to send me to Sanski Most or Prijedor but I refused because I knew I would never stay alive there. Instead, I asked to be sent to Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Because I knew that a neighbour of mine whose name I do not want to state for the sake of her safety was a nurse in the local hospital and I was sure she would help me. "Finally, the commanding officer agreed to that, even though there was a problem with fuel." I assume that Banja Luka is further away than Prijedor and Sanski Most, if you were to be taken to a hospital there. Right? "They transported me to the headquarters which was located about 15 kilometres from Poljak towards Bronzani Majdan in the direction of Banja Luka because the ambulance was there." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these Serb soldiers from your unit and their commander, whose last name is Malic, took all necessary measures for you to receive medical treatment and to be sent to a clinic first and then on to hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That practically means that the Serbs with whom you worked, among whom you moved about freely, after everything that had happened to you practically saved your life. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say, "In the morning of the 22nd of September," on the other side, I -- "they put me on a bus to Banja Luka and I finally reached the hospital that same day. I spent ten days in the hospital and was then released." Banja Luka was in Serb hands all the time. It was never taken by the Muslim forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spent ten days in hospital. You were taken care of, as much as possible during those ten days. And after that, you were released, and then later on you went to the territory that was controlled by the Muslim forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. 1047. I have no further questions -- oh, I beg your pardon. Just one more question. One more question. I omitted to mention that. I didn't find this clear. You said that they had said to you that they would spare your lives if you gave them 5.000 Deutschmark each. That seems illogical to me. If they wanted to kill you and if they wanted to take away your money, they could have taken your money irrespective of whether they killed you or not. Is there some kind of confusion there, or is it something that I'm missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1047
